subject: Question about Polychoric correlation and p-value of RMSEA

messages.author: ed1512e85556685e
messages.subject: Question about Polychoric correlation and p-value of RMSEA
parts:
Greeting, 

I have a dataset with about 1200 complete subjects. There are 23 manifested indicators in my dataset, all of those indicators are 4-point Likert like scale. 
After a long self studied, I think that I should use polychoric correlation instead of Pearson's correlation (due to ordinal scale of manifest indicators)
I used R and ran EFA using psych package which suggest 6 factors. I specified the model and cfa command in lavaan as followed...

model <- 'F1 =~ x1+x2+x3+x4
                F2 =~ x5+x6+x7
                F3 =~ x8+x9
                F4 =~ x10+x11+x12+x13
                F5 =~ x14+x15+x16+x17
                F6 =~ x18+x19+x20+x21+x22+x23'
fit <- cfa(model, data=data,std.lv=T, ordered = names(data), estimator = 'wlsmv')

The robusted fit indicator for RMSEA(90%CI) and p-value are 0.065, (0.062 - 0.069), and 0.000
However, when I removed the 'ordered' part from my command p-value for RMSEA changed to 0.860.
I tried to adjust the model using modnidices which improved fit indicators for a bit, but the effect of 'ordered' is still the same (i.e., p-value changed from highly significant to unsignficant)

I would like to ask for suggestion if statistical significant of RMSEA p-value is the effect of polychoric correlation (which I guess it markedly change the correlation matrix from the data) or if my cfa command is incorrect. 

Best, 
Wisarut

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Question about Polychoric correlation and p-value of RMSEA
parts:
It is quite possible. Look at the two correlation matrices--the Pearson and the polychoric. They may be substantially different. Crude ategorization of observed variables can attenuate correlations, and the weaker correlations can reduce power, making fit seem less bad. If that is true in your case, then the Pearson-based results are untrustworthy. You might also look at the bivariate distribution of observed responses. The polychoric correlation presumes that there are underlying bivariate normal responses. If the bivariate distributions seem inconsistent with such an assumption, then the polychoric-based results may also be dubious.

Did you use the same WLSMV estimator in both cases? If you changed estimator, that might also have an efect on your results. Alternately, with lavaan, the combination of ordered + WLSMV may mean something substantially different from the combination of continuous + WLSMV.
